text: Imagine a world without a single mosquito, fly or wasp.
It sounds like paradise… but it could be one of the worst things that ever happened to life on Earth.
So what would really happen if every insect disappeared?
Let's follow the chain reaction, step by step.
First, you need to know how many there are.
Scientists have described about one million insect species. That is more than half of all known animals.
And many more are still waiting to be discovered.
Consequence one: flowers lose their messengers.
Bees, butterflies, flies and beetles carry pollen from flower to flower.
Without that help, many plants cannot make fruit or seeds.
According to a major UN-backed report, about three quarters of the leading food crops rely, at least in part, on animal pollinators.
Apples, strawberries, almonds, coffee… even chocolate.
We would not starve right away. Wheat, rice and corn are pollinated by the wind. But our plates would become much poorer.
Consequence two: a hungry food chain.
Most songbirds feed insects to their chicks. So do many bats, frogs, lizards and freshwater fish.
Without insects, these animals would decline. And the predators that eat them would follow.
Consequence three: nobody cleans up.
Beetles, flies and termites break down dead leaves, fallen wood, dung and dead animals.
In the nineteen sixties, Australia even brought in foreign dung beetles, because its native beetles could not handle cow dung piling up in the fields.
Without these recyclers, nutrients would stay locked in waste.
Ants and beetles also dig tunnels that let air and water into the ground.
Soils would become poorer, and plants would grow less.
Would anyone win? Probably grasses and other wind-pollinated plants.
Fungi and bacteria would take over part of the cleanup.
But the world would be quieter, less colorful, and far less diverse.
The good news: insects are not about to vanish.
But in some German nature reserves, one study measured a drop of more than seventy-five percent in flying insects, in under thirty years.
Habitat loss, pesticides and climate change are among the suspected causes.
Insects are tiny, but they hold up much of life on land.
